title: Asser’s problem
area: Database theory and finite model theory
formal:
Is the class of finite first-order spectra closed under complement within the positive integers?

For every finite relational vocabulary \(\tau\) and every first-order sentence \(\varphi\) over \(\tau\), does there exist a finite relational vocabulary \(\sigma\) and a first-order sentence \(\psi\) over \(\sigma\) such that
\[\forall n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}:\quad \bigl(\exists\text{ an }n\text{-element }\sigma\text{-structure satisfying }\psi\bigr)\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \neg\bigl(\exists\text{ an }n\text{-element }\tau\text{-structure satisfying }\varphi\bigr)?\]
The vocabulary and sentence \((\sigma,\psi)\) may depend on \((\tau,\varphi)\), but must work simultaneously for every positive size \(n\). They need not use the original vocabulary. No effective procedure for obtaining \(\psi\), or bound on its length, is required.
definitions:
Vocabulary and syntax. A finite relational vocabulary is a finite, possibly empty list \(R_1,\ldots,R_m\) of distinct relation symbols with specified positive integer arities \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\). There are no function or constant symbols. Equality is a logical symbol and is always available. Variables are drawn from a countable supply. Formulas are finite expressions built from equality atoms \(x=y\), relation atoms \(R_i(x_1,\ldots,x_{a_i})\), negation, conjunction, and first-order existential quantification; other Boolean connectives and universal quantification have their usual equivalent definitions. Variables in an atom may repeat. A sentence has no free variables. Neither the number of symbols, their arities, the number of variables nor quantifier depth has a fixed global bound.

Structures and semantics. A structure over \(\tau\) consists of a nonempty finite domain \(A\) and, for each symbol \(R_i\), an arbitrary interpretation \(R_i^A\subseteq A^{a_i}\). Equality is actual equality of elements. A relation atom holds under a variable assignment exactly when the assigned tuple belongs to its interpreted relation; equality, Boolean operations and existential quantification are evaluated in the usual way, with quantified variables ranging over elements of \(A\). Write \(\mathcal A\models\varphi\) when a sentence is true in this structure. There is no built-in order, arithmetic, graph condition or fixed interpretation of a relation. A sentence may itself require such properties.

Spectrum. Define
\[\operatorname{Spec}(\varphi)=\{n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}:\exists\mathcal A,\ |A|=n\text{ and }\mathcal A\models\varphi\}.\]
The existence quantifier ranges over all interpretations of all symbols at that size. One may fix the domain to \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), since relabeling does not affect truth. The target is
\[\operatorname{Spec}(\psi)=\mathbb Z_{>0}\setminus\operatorname{Spec}(\varphi).\]
Only cardinalities are retained; the spectrum does not count how many models or isomorphism types exist at a size. Empty and infinite structures are outside this definition, and the complement does not include zero.

Scope. The restriction to relational vocabularies preserves the ordinary class of first-order spectra: finite-arity functions and constants can instead be represented by relations, together with first-order conditions enforcing their graph or unique-value interpretation on the same domain. No second-order quantifiers over relations or arbitrary external numerical predicates are added to the representing sentence. The target is an existence statement about finite formulas and their entire sets of model sizes. It imposes no computational model, sentence-construction resource bound or model-search algorithm requirement.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed universal complement-closure statement or its full logical negation. A positive proof must establish a single representing first-order sentence for the whole positive-integer complement of each input spectrum; the new vocabulary is unrestricted except for finiteness and the stated relational syntax. A negative proof must establish a first-order spectrum whose complement is not the spectrum of any first-order sentence over any permitted finite vocabulary. Equivalently, for that input sentence, every candidate representing sentence must fail at some positive size, which may depend on the candidate. Checking finitely many sizes, ruling out a fixed vocabulary or variable bound, or showing that literal sentence negation fails is insufficient. The theorem must be unconditional unless it also proves every additional assumption used.
why: A first-order sentence can describe rich finite structures, while its spectrum keeps only the possible domain sizes. Asser’s question asks whether the sizes excluded by one such description can always be the sizes admitted by another. Its equivalence with closure of nondeterministic exponential time under complement makes this a fundamental meeting point of finite model theory and computational complexity.

importance.reason: A classical foundational question of finite model theory and descriptive complexity, explicitly surveyed as an unresolved central spectrum problem. Its complement target is distinct from PTIME capture, query containment and ordinary finite satisfiability.

progress.text: Scholz introduces the spectrum question and Asser asks whether the class is closed under complement.
The nondeterministic exponential-time characterization connects complement closure to NE versus coNE.
The comprehensive survey retains the unrestricted complement question as open.
Two-variable logic with counting receives an exact semilinear spectrum characterization and complement closure.
The general complement question reduces to three-variable binary-relation inputs despite an infinite variable hierarchy.
The reduction is refined to three-variable inputs whose models are undirected bipartite graphs.
The journal article on ultimately periodic counting gives an effective Presburger description of spectra in that two-variable extension.

context_blocks.text: Scholz asked in 1952 how to characterize the sets of finite sizes admitted by first-order sentences. Asser’s 1955 complement question asks for a particular closure property of that class. Characterizing the class in another language does not by itself settle its closure under complement; the historical survey treats these as distinct questions.

The quantifier over structures is essential. For example, over a unary predicate \(P\), the sentence \((\exists x\,P(x))\land(\exists y\,\neg P(y))\) has a model exactly at sizes at least two. Its logical negation has a model at every positive size, since \(P\) can be empty. The complement of the original spectrum is just \(\{1\}\). Thus truth of a negated sentence in some structure is different from absence of every model of the original sentence at that size.

A spectrum forgets which structures realize a size. It can be empty, finite, cofinite or infinite with large gaps. The survey records closure under finite unions and intersections, with relation vocabularies allowed to vary. Complement is the missing general Boolean closure operation. Requiring a representative in the original vocabulary would impose an additional condition not present in Asser’s question.

The computational characterization uses binary representations of sizes. If \(m\) is the number of bits in \(n\), the class \(\mathrm{NE}\) consists of languages accepted by a nondeterministic Turing machine in time \(O(2^{cm})\) for some fixed constant \(c\). Jones and Selman, and independently Fagin, identify first-order spectra with the sets whose canonical binary representations belong to this class. Here a canonical positive representation begins with a one and has no leading zeros.

Consequently, general spectrum complement closure is equivalent to \(\mathrm{NE}=\mathrm{coNE}\), where the latter class contains complements of languages in \(\mathrm{NE}\). The input-size convention matters: unary encoding has length \(n\), whereas binary encoding has length proportional to \(\log n\). The relevant complexity class is single-exponential nondeterministic time in that binary length, not polynomial time in an explicitly supplied structure.

A negative answer would also imply \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{coNP}\), and therefore \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), as noted in the two-variable paper. The converse is not asserted. This is a precise one-way connection to those complexity questions, not an identification of Asser’s problem with P versus NP.

For two-variable logic with counting, denoted \(C^2\), Kopczyński and Tan prove a complete answer: its spectra are exactly the semilinear sets and are closed under complement even within \(C^2\). This logic reuses only two variable names, with quantifiers asserting that at least a fixed number of elements satisfy a formula. In one dimension, semilinear sets are ultimately periodic: beyond a finite threshold, membership depends only on the residue modulo some positive period.

The variable-hierarchy paper shows that allowing more variables genuinely increases spectrum expressibility along an infinite hierarchy. Nevertheless, its complement problem reduces to input sentences with only three variables and binary relations. These are different claims: a reduction of the complement question does not say that every spectrum itself has a three-variable description. The complement representative in that reduction may use arbitrarily many variables.

The 2018 paper sharpens the reduction further to input sentences using three variables and one symmetric binary relation, all of whose models are undirected bipartite graphs. Its encoding changes model sizes by a fixed affine transformation. The resulting equivalence still asks whether each restricted input spectrum’s complement is some first-order spectrum; it does not require a three-variable bipartite representative for that complement.

The 2024 paper extends the two-variable spectrum analysis to ultimately periodic counting conditions. Its Theorem 9.1 effectively describes finite model sizes by a formula of Presburger arithmetic, the first-order arithmetic of addition and order. That is substantive progress for an expressive restricted logic. It does not remove the two-variable restriction or settle complement closure for arbitrary first-order sentences.

Finite satisfiability asks whether a sentence has any finite model at all; Asser’s problem asks about the entire set of its possible finite sizes. The known undecidability of the former does not refute the latter’s non-effective existence claim. Likewise, a positive answer here would not, by itself, provide a decision procedure for finite satisfiability.

source_formulation.text: Preserves importance 96 and Asser’s general complement question, with nonempty finite models, positive-integer complement and a new unrestricted finite vocabulary for the representing sentence. No effective complementation algorithm or bounded-length representative is added. The three-variable reductions in the cited papers require the complement to be an unrestricted first-order spectrum; they do not require its representative to remain in the restricted fragment or prove that every spectrum already belongs to that fragment.

sentences: The spectrum of a first-order sentence is the set of positive sizes of its finite models.
Asser’s problem asks whether the complement of every such set is again a first-order spectrum.
The representing sentence may use a new vocabulary and must work at all sizes simultaneously, with no effective construction required.
The general question is equivalent to closure of nondeterministic single-exponential time under complement for binary-encoded sizes.
Two-variable counting spectra are understood, while reductions to three-variable graph inputs and later restricted-logic results leave the general question open.
